html:
Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish writer and clergyman, born in Dublin in 1667, best known for Gulliver's Travels of 1726.

He was dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin from 1713. Gulliver's Travels, a satire on human pride, politics and science dressed as a tale of voyages, has been read by children and adults ever since. In A Modest Proposal of 1729 he suggested, with a straight face, that the Irish poor sell their babies as food to the rich, a savage attack on English policy and Irish landlords.

He also wrote pamphlets urging the Irish to buy only Irish goods. Though a Protestant of the ruling class, he became a hero to the Dublin poor. He left money to found a hospital for the mentally ill. His friends included Alexander Pope. See Ireland and the Protestant Ascendancy.
